Following immediately by the push crew asking me to release the brakes so they can adjust the tow bar which I acknowledged brakes released. Within a few seconds I feel the aircraft moving so I applied the breaks and at which time I hear tow bar is released set the brakes which I already did but not in time for the nose tire to make contact with the tow bar. We contacted maintainer to come out to inspect the plane they found every was normal and no damage and we returned to the Gate to make a log book entry and maintenance signed it off as everything was normal no damage found. We did proceeded to ZZZ. Cause: Inexperience push crew and that I the captain should have kept the brakes set if they were asking me to release to adjust the tow bar I should have told them we will have maintenance come out to handle any adjustments.
ASRSN:2195634.s: During pushback, the captain released brakes to allow the push crew to adjust the tow bar, causing the nose tire to strike the bar before brakes were reapplied. Maintenance found no damage, but the captain attributed the incident to the push crew's inexperience and his own failure to keep brakes set.

ASRSN:2195639.n: Upon climbout I noticed excessive forward force required to maintain target pitch. I noticed the electric pitch trim was unresponsive. I asked the non flying pilot to check the force required to maintain target pitch. He concurred. He continued to fly the aircraft. He reduced power to slow the plane and reduce the tail forces. After that was accomplished the aircraft was manageable using the manual trim wheel. I [requested priority handling] to ATC and asked for return vectors for the airport. We elected to climb an additional 1000 ft. to give us a buffer from terrain. We proceeded to fly a long downwind in the valley away from terrain and populated areas. This gave us time to trouble shoot and run checklists. After agreeing to return to the airport I set up the ILS approach for Runway XXL the longest Runway. We also briefed our overweight landing condition and transfer of controls after landing. We configured and managed the jet using manual trim. We landed at 1.2 vertical acceleration and less than -400 FPM. We taxied in to the FBO under our own power without assistance and shutdown without incident. We took off from Runway XX, during the climb the pilot flying noticed the trim appeared to not be working. He initially thought it was a jammed flight control. He asked me to check mine and I noticed and enormous amount of pressure required to lower the nose of the plane but I was able to control the plane. I elected to slow the plane while at the same time he was pulling out the AFM. Since we had no message on the EICAS and were not 100% sure yet what it was, I continued to fly. I used the trim wheel to bring the plane back to a manageable pressure and told him we would be going back to ZZZ. He [requested priority handling] and we got vectors downwind. We wanted a long final and to be away from the city and population for configuration changes. After coming to the conclusion this was only the trim not working and we could use the trim wheel for all our changes we asked for XXL because we were over weight and it's the longest Runway. He ran all the checklist and got us set up to use the ILS to help with stabilization. We briefed the approach and that we would do the handover of controls as we passed 60 kt as we used to do in the airlines. We started to configure about 20 miles off the end of XXL and came in on a very stabilized approach. Right before touchdown I asked him to note the VSI. We slowed and taxied off the Runway with no incident and 1.2 on the vertical accelerometer.
ASRSN:2195639.s: Pilots experienced unresponsive electric pitch trim and excessive control forces during climbout, requiring manual trim wheel operation. They returned to the airport for a stabilized ILS approach on the longest runway, landing safely with 1.2 G vertical acceleration and no further incident.

ASRSN:2195642.n: GPS interference experienced in Sofia, Ankara, and Baku FIRs.
ASRSN:2195642.s: Pilots reported GPS interference while operating in the Sofia, Ankara, and Baku FIRs. The narrative does not specify the aircraft type, flight phase, cause, or outcome of the interference.

ASRSN:2195688.n: On postflight in ZZZ I noticed 4 boxes of human tissue" sitting on the edge of the belt loader. I went to take a look to see if any hazmat was about to be loaded when a Ramp per said, "Ohhhhhh somebody is in trouble. These were supposed to be left in ZZZ1." I learned they were in the aft cargo. We pulled the weight and balance for our flight from ZZZ1 and it is no surprise that this cargo was undocumented. It amounted to 243 pounds of undeclared weight on the aircraft.Suggestions: Have ramp personnel check aft cargo bin, or have flight crew check aft cargo bins, or both." When Person A did walkaround after flight ZZZ1 - ZZZ. He noticed 4 packages 40 pounds each being unloaded from the aft cargo. These were supposed to be unloaded in ZZZ1. The ground crew there missed taking these off. That was on [the previous] flight. This resulted in an incorrect weight and balance from ZZZ1 to ZZZ since it wasn't recorded we had anything in the aft.
ASRSN:2195688.s: Ramp personnel failed to unload 243 pounds of human tissue at ZZZ1, leaving it in the aft cargo for the flight to ZZZ. This undocumented weight caused an incorrect weight and balance calculation for the flight.

ASRSN:2195699.n: The coffee machine exploded when we were doing the initial and it burned me all over my face and body. Coffee grinds all over my face and body. I went to disarm the door as soon as the ding came on and I remember doing the grit bar but second guessing the ribbon because as I was getting up my arm started to throb, and I recall getting up and trying to ice it the captain was aware of everything even came out and saw the machine and was amazed how bad it was. When we landed, I disarmed my door properly...when I got home I started to second guess myself If I cross checked the 1r door. I remember going to door and verifying but at the same time my co worker was burned by the coffee maker and she was still in pain and I asked her if she was okay. I am not sure if I verified the red strap.
ASRSN:2195699.s: A cabin crew member was burned by an exploding coffee machine during the initial phase of flight. While the Captain observed the incident, the reporter later expressed uncertainty about whether they properly verified the red strap while disarming the door upon landing.

ASRSN:2195841.n: Took off out of ZZZ. Upon passing 2500 feet the engine shuttered once and then once more. Instructor took control of the airplane and turned around back to the airport. Throttle was stuck on decent, and upon the threshold of the runway instructor cut the mixture to land. Landed safely, and coasted off the runway. No injuries, and no damage to person or property.
ASRSN:2195841.s: A pilot and instructor experienced two engine shudders at 2,500 feet after takeoff from ZZZ due to a throttle stuck in descent. The instructor took control, cut the mixture on the runway threshold, and landed safely with no injuries or damage.

ASRSN:2195845.n: Prior to departure checked for traffic on final visually and ADS-B traffic on the MFD and no traffic was observed (distance ring on the MFD was set to 2.5 miles). While turning crosswind and climbing from ~800 ft to pattern altitude we noticed a traffic conflict appear on the G1000 and received a traffic audio traffic alert. The traffic was nearly the same altitude flying westbound through the DYB traffic pattern on the south side of the airport. I immediately took control of the plane and executed an evasive maneuver to the right to slow convergence of the aircraft and determined the best altitude was to climb. Once we no longer had a risk to flight safety we obtained the call sign from the G1000 and I re-entered the pattern and executed a landing. Prior to starting turn to crosswind there was no evidence of the traffic on the G1000 and with the plane behind us were unable to acquire visually. We did make calls before departure indicating runway and remaining in the pattern and made a call turning crosswind. Aircraft X started near Ladson and ended shortly after the NMAC. I didn't pick up again until the plane was SE of Atlanta. Why the plane was flying at pattern altitude directly through the DYB traffic pattern with no radio calls is unknown. They also did not appear to make any evasive maneuvers.
ASRSN:2195845.s: The pilot of a G1000-equipped aircraft climbing from 800 ft to pattern altitude at DYB received a traffic alert and executed a right evasive maneuver to avoid a westbound aircraft at the same altitude. The other aircraft, which made no radio calls or evasive maneuvers, was flying directly through the traffic pattern, causing a near mid-air collision.

ASRSN:2195849.n: I was on a left base for TMB 27L when tower advised of Aircraft X to the north on a right base for 27R. After turning final for TMB 27L, I received a traffic alert from tower of Aircraft X converging and suggested a climb to avoid collision. I initiated a climb and gained visual with the aircraft. Aircraft X established on final next to me for 27L before vectoring northwest back towards 27R. After I landed, Aircraft X circled back over the field to the south through the pattern for 27L before gaining awareness of which runway was 27R. After shutdown I called the tower and confirmed Aircraft X was directed to land on runway 27R and not to enter the final or pattern for 27L.
ASRSN:2195849.s: The pilot on final for TMB 27L climbed after tower advised of converging Aircraft X on a right base for 27R. Aircraft X mistakenly entered the 27L pattern before being vectored back to 27R, which the pilot confirmed was the intended runway.

ASRSN:2195853.n: Operating in area marked as used for extensive training conducting skidding stall training. During a debrief aircraft was placed in a gentle continuous turn to the left (10 to 15 degrees AOB (angle of bank)) when aircraft was seen at same altitude, opposite direction just left of the nose. Turned right to avoid and saw that it appeared to be a general aviation aircraft from Falcon Field. ADSB In system had not shown the aircraft in advance however it did appear shortly after. Broadcast again on common frequency of multiple aircraft conducting spin and stall training in the area and informed other aircraft in the vicinity of the aircraft so no further events would occur.
ASRSN:2195853.s: A pilot conducting skidding stall training encountered a general aviation aircraft from Falcon Field while in a left turn. The pilot executed a right turn to avoid the conflict after the intruder appeared on ADSB In, then broadcast a warning to other training aircraft in the area.

ASRSN:2195856.n: I was on my local student pilot solo. I was coming back into my home airport, ZZZ, and was making a landing on runway XX. My first attempt at landing was unstable so I performed a go around. On the second attempt, my approach was better. However, right upon landing I encountered a gusting crosswind. I attempted to correct, but I rolled off the runway to the left side into the grass. During the runway excursion, I did not hit anything and I was able to maneuver the plane back onto the runway. I taxied the plane back to the school. Our maintenance team from the school inspected the plane and found no damage. One of my Private Pilot students was performing their local solo this morning. All went as planned until returning to land on Runway XX. While they were out flying winds shifted and became gusty. During the first attempt to land the student decided their approach was unstable and initiated a go-around. During the second attempt to land the student opted to continue the approach and was caught off guard by a gust as or near the touch down point. This resulted in a runway excursion on the left side of Runway XX. The student was able to regain control of the aircraft, guide it back onto the landing surface, and return to the ramp area. No damage was done to airport property. After inspection by maintenance, the aircraft was determined to have suffered no damage.
ASRSN:2195856.s: A student pilot soloing at ZZZ experienced a runway excursion to the left on Runway XX during a second landing attempt due to a gusting crosswind. The pilot regained control, returned the aircraft to the runway, and maintenance confirmed no damage to the plane or airport property.

ASRSN:2195859.n: Sold an aircraft a year ago, I had flown it many years from ZZZ, uncontrolled, avionics original, steam, used hand held mic. Renting Aircraft X with headset and PTT and Garmin 430. About 10 hrs renting. Generally when taxing to Runway 32 told take Zulu/Alpha to runway. This time told taxi 32 via Alpha. On Alpha and when I got to Zulu was confused for a moment and started down Zulu, I find arrows on signage at Zulu/Alpha intersection unclear, crossed limit line that is about 25 yards from runway, thought cleared to cross to get to runup. Knew not cleared onto runway and would not have entered without clearance, saw Aircraft Y on about 2 mile final. I was never a threat to Aircraft Y. Trying to confirm I had made correct turn, realized I hadn't and turned to go back to continue correctly. Ground called my N number after I was already turning back and I replied 'sorry I had made a wrong turn.' Proceeded to runup and take off without incident. Told later they told Aircraft Y to go around, if I was threat to Aircraft Y why didn't they tell me to stop as I went down Zulu?
ASRSN:2195859.s: A pilot renting Aircraft X at an uncontrolled field mistakenly crossed a runway limit line while taxiing to Runway 32 due to unclear signage. Although the pilot corrected the error and took off without incident, Air Traffic Control instructed an arriving aircraft to go around.

ASRSN:2195883.n: My student and I were on a night VFR XC (ZZZ1-ZZZ1 via ZZZ2)He needed to fulfil some extra night hours for his commercial requirements so we stopped by ZZZ airport on the way back for a touch and go.Whilst on a long final for Runway XX at ZZZ my student was far too high so, since there was no traffic in the area, I advised we spiral down to an altitude from which we could make a stablised approach.After one 360 turn the VASI was still showing two white lights so I said to do another turn. Halfway through the second turn I realised our height AGL over our specific location was quite low so I told him to power up and continue on the approach. We were still on glide path referencing the VASI, but I fear we may have descended below 1000 AGL, and since we were over a congested area it's possible we temporarily did not meet the requirements of 91.119. In the future I believe I need to have an awareness of our height AGL whilst at low altitudes during an approach to ensure I meet the requirements of 91.119, especially given that at night your sense of height can be distorted.
ASRSN:2195883.s: An instructor and student in a night VFR flight descended below 1000 AGL over a congested area while performing two 360-degree turns to correct a high approach at ZZZ airport. The instructor attributed the potential 91.119 violation to distorted night height perception and the need for better altitude awareness during low-level maneuvers.

ASRSN:2195906.n: As I was taxiing to Runway XX for an IFR departure, I began to drift left of center line. To correct for this, I began to add right rudder. Due to my low power setting and slow speed, I lost rudder authority and continued to veer to the left. As a I continued add more rudder and right brake, I did not have a normal braking and turning response and realized I was going to exit the taxiway into the grass. In that moment, I pulled mixture and began to brake with the left foot pedal which resulted in me exiting the taxiway. No damage occurred to the airport taxiway, taxiway lights or signs, nor was the airplane damaged in any way.
ASRSN:2195906.s: The pilot drifted left while taxiing for an IFR departure due to low power and slow speed, which caused a loss of rudder authority. Despite applying right rudder and brakes, the aircraft exited the taxiway into the grass, resulting in no damage to the airplane or airport infrastructure.

ASRSN:2195910.n: Tower informed us of a possible drone reporting and asked us to keep an eye one. Once vectored onto final for an ASR (Airport Surveillance Radar) [approach] RWY 15, Instructor Pilot (IP) noticed a white flashing light at the 2 o'clock position. IP reported to tower and were informed a helicopter was in that location. While communicating with Tower IP noticed a second flashing white light between the reported helo traffic and our aircraft. Light appeared to be less than .5 miles away and about 500 ft higher than our airftacts altitude. IP queried tower if there was other traffic in the area and Tower reported 'negative'. No colored position lights could be seen on the object with only a flashing white light visible and moving in the opposite direction of our aircraft. Tower Controllers continued the ASR but forgot to inform the aircraft to decend. We arrived at 2000ft at the MAP and Tower told us to execute missed approach and informed all aircraft the airspace was now closed in order to sanitize the airspace.
ASRSN:2195910.s: During an ASR approach to RWY 15, the Instructor Pilot observed an unidentified flashing white light while Tower incorrectly identified nearby traffic as a helicopter. The controller failed to issue a descent clearance, leading to a missed approach and airspace closure to sanitize the area.

ASRSN:2195914.n: We were on radar vector for landing runway 9 at MIA airport, following another traffic ahead of us. During vector we were assigned speed, but I think we were too close during separation , and the traffic took so long to get off the runway , so finally the tower told us to go around and fly heading 140 and maintain 3000 feet, but with that heading we got TCAS RA with some traffic below. I think it could've been better for us if they gave us runway heading and 3000 feet. We performed the maneuver according to our SOP.
ASRSN:2195914.s: The flight crew on a radar vector for MIA Runway 9 executed a go-around due to slow traffic clearance, receiving a heading of 140 and 3000 feet. This clearance resulted in a TCAS RA with traffic below, which the crew resolved by following SOPs while suggesting a runway heading would have been safer.

ASRSN:2195919.n: I was flying a practice RNAV09 instrument approach to Ramona, CA (RNM)using a view limiting device. My heading was approximately 090. While on the approach, another plane took off from RNM on a westbound heading. The Ramona tower called the approaching traffic. The safety pilot saw the plane and reported traffic in site to the tower. He thought it was on track to pass off to the right of us so he told me to steer left, which I did.The Ramona tower observed us turning left, which appeared to put us more on a collision course with the approaching traffic. When the controller called again, I noted the urgency of the call and removed the view limiting device. I saw the approaching traffic and that the correct evasive action was a right turn, which I immediately executed and we passed by the approaching traffic without further incident.I know that in almost all cases, a turn to the right is the correct evasive maneuver when planes are approaching each other head on so when the safety pilot told me to turn left I should have immediately removed the view limiting device so that I could do my own assessment of the situation and determine the correct course of action.
ASRSN:2195919.s: A pilot conducting a practice RNAV09 approach to Ramona (RNM) with a view-limiting device turned left on safety pilot advice, increasing collision risk with a departing aircraft. The pilot removed the device, executed a correct right turn, and avoided the conflict, noting the safety pilot's initial instruction was contrary to standard head-on avoidance procedures.

ASRSN:2195929.n: On a VFR flight from ZZZ to AUO, I picked up the weather at Auburn about 30 miles out, informed ATC I had the weather and I was ready to cancel flight following. They told me to squawk VFR and frequency change approved. I switched to the Auburn CTAF frequency and reported my position as I approached the airport. As I was entering the downwind for Runway 36, Auburn Tower contacted me on the CTAF frequency, notified me I violated their airspace and gave me their frequency to switch to. They gave me a landing clearance and I landed without issue.This is a flight I have made multiple times, and before the flight I updated my sectional chart and checked the airport NOTAMs before departure. At no point in that process did I realize a Tower had been added to this airport. After landing, I checked the sectional and saw that the airport is shown in class E/G airspace, with the icon being red, which indicates an untowered field. The NOTAMs do not warn that the airport is towered, but there are two NOTAMs mentioning times the Tower is closed. I must have skimmed over these because NOTAMs mentioning a Tower being closed should be irrelevant to an untowered airport.I told the Tower Controller that my updated sectional showed the airport as untowered, and he responded that 'it's on there.' After reviewing it post-flight, I disagree, and I would be surprised if any VFR pilot looking at the airport on a sectional would realize it has a Tower.
ASRSN:2195929.s: A VFR pilot flying to Auburn entered the downwind for Runway 36 on the CTAF frequency, unaware the airport had a tower. The pilot violated controlled airspace because the sectional chart depicted the field as untowered and NOTAMs did not clearly indicate tower operations.

ASRSN:2196009.n: We were in the North Port at taxi lane C and were told to follow our company. They began to taxi forward and I was keeping the interval tight with my taxi light on. As they turned right onto G, I noticed lights from my left which were rapidly approaching. I stopped the aircraft since it was apparent that the other aircraft was not stopping. It was [another air carrier] aircraft, that split our section. If I would not have stopped, he would have hit our aircraft at the speed he was taxiing. We tried repeatedly to inform Ground, and were finally able to get our own taxi instructions since we were no longer able to follow [the company aircraft]. The [other] aircraft either did not see us or did not care.
ASRSN:2196009.s: The pilot stopped their aircraft on taxiway G at North Port to avoid a collision with another carrier's aircraft that failed to stop while splitting the taxi section. The reporter attributed the incident to the other pilot either not seeing them or disregarding their presence, forcing a request for new taxi instructions.

ASRSN:2196014.n: We were taxiing southbound on taxiway A. A minivan, company markings not clear, crossed taxiway A right in front of us, and was close to collision. We had to apply brakes. No injuries. We reported the incident to the Ground Controller.
ASRSN:2196014.s: While taxiing southbound on taxiway A, the crew applied brakes to avoid a near-collision with a minivan that crossed the taxiway directly in front of the aircraft. The incident resulted in no injuries and was reported to the Ground Controller.

ASRSN:2196058.n: On the ZZZZZX arrival, we were given relief of all speed restrictions when descending via. Approximately 24000 ft. an extremely bright white light emanated from the top of the windshield and became larger and brighter. Initially I thought we were hit by an extremely bright and powerful laser, much stronger than a typical pen laser, but shortly realized this was a window arc that turned into something so bright I have not experienced before. I have had several window arc events in my career and at least 2-3 window delaminations. This was something much more severe. Fearing for my First Officer's (FO's) immediate safety, I immediately removed the power source from the window, and the bright light almost immediately reduced in intensity. After a minute of discussing what actually occurred, my FO thought it was a fire, there was a very loud boom and immediately I saw the windshield cracked severely. I pulled out the QRH, advised ATC and [requested priority handling]. I also asked to be given headings to fly and altitudes and to be taken off the arrival. After pulling out the QRH the FO ascertained the outer pane was broken and the inner pane was undamaged. I followed the QRH and worked radios while the FO continued flying. After completing the QRH, and further into the arrival, I advised FO due to his windshield cracks that I would be doing the landing. I also advised the FO to put his goggles on in case the windshield became further damaged, at least he would have extra eye protection. We landed uneventfully, wrote up the event, talked to Maintenance in ZZZ, I called Maintenance Control, and then the duty pilot to provide additional info.Suggestions: I thought we handled the situation as good as we could have. During the descent in arrival at flight level 240, I noticed a small dot of light on the upper corner of my windshield, which gradually became bigger, brighter, and appeared similar to fire on wire. Whole cockpit was bright. Imagining various possibilities such as traffic or an external light source, I soon realized this was not the case. It was something like electrical fire. It was something bright and also melting texture.We were maintaining a speed of 290-300 kts., with the speed restriction previously deleted by ATC. The Captain decided to turn off the window heat for the R1 window. Approximately 30 seconds later, we heard a noise akin to an explosion like BOMm" and the window cracked. In response, I grabbed my O2 mask and we [requested priority handling], after QRH requested vectors for ILS XX at ZZZ Airport. The situation was managed smoothly thereafter. As the First Officer and pilot flying (PF), I transferred control to the Captain and donned my smoke goggles to protect my eyes if something else happened."
ASRSN:2196058.s: During the ZZZZZX arrival at FL240, the Captain and First Officer experienced a severe window arc on the R1 windshield that caused the outer pane to crack after the Captain cut window heat. The crew followed the QRH, requested priority handling, and landed safely with the Captain taking control for the approach.

ASRSN:2196096.n: On climbout we had a inflight medical emergency, a passenger was having seizures, foaming at the mouth and was not conscious. We [advised ATC ] and exercised our authority to expedite our return to Chicago ORD. From the time we got the call to over the threshold was a very quick experience. We got the visual approach to 27C in ORD loaded, briefed, descent checklist completed, and landing data setup. ATC asked if we were ready to turn base and the FO said he was ready. I had been flying with him for the last two days, so I was confident in his abilities. We accepted to the short base turn to final and the FO started to slow and configure the aircraft. The first thing that caught my attention was the FO bugged 2,200 feet in the altitude selection. While that is the FAF altitude, that wouldn't be normal for Chicago. We got established on the visual approach, and into green needles. All seemed normal at this point and I called the FA to get a quick update on the passenger. I was informed he was still 'out', I said OK we're going to be on the ground very soon and paramedics are going to meet us at the gate. The FO called for gear down flaps 30 and I configured the aircraft as requested. I noticed the boards were still deployed, we got those retracted. I don't remember what speed we were at but I happened to look at the radar altimeter and it was 900 something. I said hey we're not fully configured and the FO said something along the lines of I'm trying to keep the speed up. I told him to slow and we put flaps 45 in. I made the decision to continue the approach due to the unconscious passenger and the aircraft being in a safe position to land.Cause:I believe the main factor was the confusion in how fast to fly and for how long. This was not briefed and a failure on my part. The FO and I had the best intentions on helping the passenger. After landing and discussing the event, I found out my FO used to fly medical flights and was not uncommon to slow extremely late. After learning this knowledge I believe my FO felt he was doing the right thing. My choice to call the Flight Attendant late while in a critical phase was also a mistake that lead to my attention to lapse. Although most of the conversion between myself and the FA was below 18,000 ft just by nature of the emergency.Suggestions:I would have stopped him from bugging 2,200. Instead I would have had him bug 4,000 like normal for Chicago. I believe when we crossed the FAF at 2200 and caught the glide slope, I lost situational awareness and believed we were at 4,000 at JMBBO. Calling the flight attendant late was not required and only added to me not noticing the FO was choosing to not slow. PM Duties.Passenger had a seizure, CA made the decision to turn back to ORD requesting 27C.Once received the flight controls stated that I was going to fly a High speed profile as the gathered information we had from the FA's (flight attendant) was that passenger seemed very Ill and passed out.Received vectors and altitude clearances from ATC accordingly, briefed and joined the LOC at high speed, I stated that I was going to keep the speed up and delay configuration which I did, but ended putting flaps 45 at 1,000 AGL resulting in a late configuration. CA was super busy getting the 2 in 2 out information so he might have not processed well my intention of keeping speed up, precluding him to preventing me or queuing me to configure sooner.Cause:Rush from an ill passenger emergency, misinterpretation of emergency authority.Suggestions:Illustrate Crews on CA emergency Authority do and dont's.
ASRSN:2196096.s: During a climbout medical emergency involving a seizing passenger, the crew expedited a return to Chicago ORD. The First Officer delayed configuration and flew a high-speed profile due to the urgency, resulting in a late flap 45 selection at 1,000 feet AGL, though the aircraft landed safely.

ASRSN:2196119.n: After leveling at FL280 and while accelerating to cruise airspeed the First Officer (FO) and I heard a loud boom followed by a slight yaw to the left. Engine 1 was spooling down and number 2 had seized. I called engine 1 out, had the FO start a descent to 10,000 and a turn to return to ZZZ. I [requested priority handling] with ATC and notified the Flight Attendant (FA) and passengers. I ran QRH. I completed the QRH and configured FMS and briefed the approach. I sent an ACARS to Dispatch and called ZZZ operations. These tasks were completed as we approached the ZZZ terminal area. A restart was not considered due to 0 n2 rotation. We landed and stopped on a taxiway to have the emergency personnel determine it was safe to taxi to the gate. The decision to return to ZZZ was supported by time to accomplish tasks, distance and time. We accepted our first vector from Approach 14 minutes after the engine failure. No injuries to my knowledge. After parking and deplaning pax I called Dispatch and chief pilot. I pulled flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) circuit breakers and called Maintenance to make appropriate log book entries. We also had a traffic advisory to work through as we were flying vectors to final. We landed using ILS XXR.
ASRSN:2196119.s: The Captain and First Officer experienced a loud boom and yaw at FL280 when Engine 1 spooled down and Engine 2 seized. They returned to ZZZ, landed safely on ILS XXR with no injuries, and attributed the failure to zero N2 rotation preventing a restart.

ASRSN:2196126.n: Single engine landing. Delayed due to Mx (Maintenance) repair on engine-driven hydraulic pump. I was the PF for the leg. On climb out, captain spotted the oil quantity showing 0" flashing in green and oil pressure nearing at its lower limit in the green arc so we leveled off at FL260. After discussing with Mx, captain promptly made a decision to divert to ZZZ. ATC gave us HDG 240 then 200 and ALT FL200 and 10,000 pilot discretion. Then, ATC gave us direct ZZZZZ for ZZZZZ arrival and as we were descending, oil pressure slowly decreased with intermittently showing green and yellow. Prior to reaching ZZZZZ, a message for OIL QUANTITY LOW showed and directed to go THRUST LEVER #1 IDLE and it disappeared after we did as instructed. Near ZZZZZ, a message appeared again with an amber LAND ASAP and we shut down ENGINE #1 as a part of the message actions as we were getting vectors for the ILS approach on runway XXL. We landed with a single engine under max landing weight and no further issues were encountered." FO's leg. During climb out at appx. FL250, I noticed an 'ADV' (Advisory) message on the engine display with a flashing 0.0 oil quantity on the number 1 engine and the oil pressure near the lower end of the green range. I attempted to contact Maintenance and dispatch on XXX.XX but we were getting out of radio range. Made the decision that we would not continue the crossing and requested to level off and get vectors back toward ZZZ. Dispatch called over the Satcom and I advised of the situation. They asked us to bring the plane back to ZZZ. During the descent, the engine continued to operate normally however, the oil pressure continued to trend downward with an occasional low oil pressure message and master caution. When we leveled off at 10,000', we got the low oil pressure message master warning to shutdown the engine. After the number 1 thrust lever came back to idle, the message cleared so we opted to keep it running at flight idle. Eventually the message returned, driving us to shut down the number 1 engine approaching ZZZZZ intersection. Continued the flight on one engine and landed in ZZZ under max landing weight without further issue.
ASRSN:2196126.s: The First Officer and Captain diverted to ZZZ during climb due to Engine 1 low oil quantity and pressure. They shut down Engine 1 near ZZZZZ following a LAND ASAP message and landed safely on a single engine at maximum landing weight.

ASRSN:2196175.n: We landed in ZZZ with a huge slam. We hit the ground so hard passengers screaming. Many children were very scared. My body lifted and smashed back down in the jump seat fully buckled in and in brace position. My back lower back is currently hurting while seated and standing. Very unfortunate for all on board.
ASRSN:2196175.s: Cabin crew reported a hard landing at ZZZ that caused passengers to scream and the crew member to be thrown against the jump seat despite being buckled in brace position. The impact resulted in lower back pain for the reporter and significant distress for passengers, including children.

ASRSN:2196186.n: During landing right before the plane touched down the door handle at the 1L door lifted about 8 inches into the opening position because the sound of air coming in like the door seemed to be cracked. This happened while I was secure in my jumpseat... I was about to push the door handle back down and notified the Captain of what happened. Flight Attendant (FA) sitting at 1R saw and two first class passengers heard the air coming in.Also early in the flight shortly after takeoff the Captain mentioned that there was a sensor saying the door was either unlocked or open, even though the door was armed and the locking indicator said it was locked.
ASRSN:2196186.s: During landing, the 1L door handle lifted 8 inches, causing an air leak heard by the crew and passengers. The Captain also reported an early flight sensor warning of an unlocked door despite the locking indicator showing it was locked.

ASRSN:2196218.n: We finished the demo and started to smell the fumes. Passengers started to ring their call lights. We smelled it really strong throughout the cabin. The number 1, me, called the Captain and informed him of this. He said to wait a few minutes for it to go away it did but then it came back worse and we called the Captain again he said we will be going back to the gate to have Maintenance to check it out. It got worse upon return to the gate. Once we opened the door the mechanics were waiting and immediately said they could smell the fumes pouring out into the jet bridge from the forward boarding door. Suggestions: Aircraft needs to be taken out of service and seriously gone over by the mechanics.
ASRSN:2196218.s: Cabin crew reported strong fumes in the cabin during the post-demo phase, prompting a return to the gate. Mechanics confirmed fumes pouring from the forward door upon arrival, leading the crew to recommend taking the aircraft out of service for inspection.

ASRSN:2196223.n: I had finished serving and checking on passengers when I heard a low boom and a silent feel about the cabin, I knew something was wrong so I began securing galley and soon the Captain called and reported that we had an engine loss , but expected a normal landing. I turned on cabin lights and read the announcement bulletin and also began to read some of the planned landing pointing out that it is just a precautionary landing. I secured cabin, dimmed lights and had a successful landing. Passengers were all fine and thankful. I did not mention engine failure.
ASRSN:2196223.s: A cabin crew member reported an engine loss during the cruise phase, indicated by a low boom and silent feel. The crew secured the cabin and prepared for a precautionary landing, which was successful with no injuries, though the passenger announcement omitted the engine failure.

ASRSN:2196240.n: Aircraft pushed back from outstation and had a HYD #1 EDP caution after start, performed QRH instead of writing up known defect or contacting maintenance control, operated entire flight to ZZZ with just ACMP, upon landing received T.R. operational delays and a 'complete failure of system 1' per write-up. Cause: pilot followed QRH instead of contacting maintenance control. QRH states switch to ACMP for system 1, fault extinguished and QRH states 'END' so pilot proceeded with flight. Suggestions: proper protocols were not followed.
ASRSN:2196240.s: The pilot operated the aircraft from an outstation to ZZZ with a HYD #1 EDP caution, following the QRH to switch to the ACMP instead of contacting maintenance control. This resulted in a complete failure of system 1 upon landing and subsequent operational delays.

ASRSN:2196241.n: Aircraft X Diversion To ZZZ. Engine 1 oil qty low. Engine 1 oil pressure low.
ASRSN:2196241.s: Aircraft X diverted to ZZZ due to low oil quantity and low oil pressure in Engine 1.

ASRSN:2196265.n: The event was a runway incursion at ZZZ runway XX and taxiway 1 at night due to lack of situational awareness, complacency, and task management, as well as unfamiliarity with the airfield. The taxi instructions given by ground were taxiway 2 then 1 to the XYL run up area. Due to lack of familiarity with the field and darkness, I initially taxied past the run up area after turning left onto taxiway 1, resulting in the need to do a 180 turn back to the run up area. I was told to advise once run up was complete. Prior to the run up check during the initial taxi, I noticed the oil pressure gauge was towards the lower end of the acceptable range, and this soon became my primary focus. During the run up, I was satisfied with all engine indications, however, a large portion of my focus remained on engine indications after the run up was complete. After the run up check, I was instructed by ground to cross XYL, hold short of XYR and switch to tower. However, since my focus was still on my engine instruments, I left the engine page up on the G1000 MFD without referencing the moving map , and turned left onto taxiway 1, toward runway XX. This was incorrect, however during the time I mistakenly felt this was the correct direction, as taxiway 1 was the last taxiway given in the initial taxi instructions, and I incorrectly had in mind that I need to be on taxiway 1 before getting to XYL. Additionally, I was somewhat confused on my exact location after taxing past, and having to return to, the run up area. At this point, my focus was still mostly on my engine instruments, which caused me to miss the fact I crossed taxiway 3, and as I approached runway XX, I didn't take the time to verify that I was approaching the correct runway until it was too late. I was told I could cross runway XYL, and assumed that the first runway I was approaching would be XYL. I realized too late that I was about to enter the wrong runway, and crossed runway XX without clearance, causing an aircraft to go around. Furthermore, I did not hear the call the aircraft on approach made at the time, as that would have been another cue to watch for landing traffic. The only corrective action that could be taken was not coming to a stop on the active runway, as I was already past the hold short markings when I realized where I was. I was told to make a 180, cross runway XX, and cross XYL again. Only after the incursion happened did I pull up the moving map to reference the airport diagram for taxi. One of the largest contributing factors was unfamiliarity with the airfield, as was evident in missing the run up area. I believe complacency played a large role in this incident as well, as I did not feel I needed to take the time to double check my taxi routing, since the taxi instructions weren't very complex. Finally, task management was clearly a major factor, as I was focused on engine indications instead of where I was moving the aircraft. The biggest takeaway from this incident is to focus on the most critical task, and to separate tasks. There was no reason I couldn't have remained longer in the run up area looking at my engine indications until I was satisfied. There was also no reason to skip double checking taxi routing, especially at an unfamiliar field. Additionally, fatigue may have played some role, as it was towards the end of the day. There were multiple ways to avoid this incident. The first being asking for a progressive taxi from ground, as this would have eliminated any confusion about which direction to turn. The second being treating all runway crossings, no matter how routine, with complete focus and attention.
ASRSN:2196265.s: The pilot of a G1000-equipped aircraft caused a runway incursion at ZZZ at night by crossing Runway XX without clearance, forcing an aircraft to go around. The incident resulted from unfamiliarity with the airfield, poor task management while monitoring engine instruments, and complacency regarding taxi routing.

ASRSN:2196269.n: Deviation over altitude in controled airspace.XA:21 pm local time.Confused meters and feet measurements.Flight using DJI flight software.Took off at XA:21 pm local tim. Took drone to 117 meters (383 feet). I thought I was at 117 feet. My permit issued by ZZZ airport was for 200 feet. I should have been more familiar with my remote measurements before flight. Next flight I will follow a pre-flight checklist provided [by a] Community Based Organization.
ASRSN:2196269.s: A drone pilot operating under a ZZZ airport permit for 200 feet inadvertently flew to 383 feet due to confusing meters with feet in DJI flight software. The pilot attributed the controlled airspace deviation to unfamiliarity with remote measurements and plans to use a pre-flight checklist for future flights.

ASRSN:2196284.n: Needed to return to gate after pushback due to brake pressure issue. At gate, tug team asked for brakes to be set, Captain responded with 'brakes set, pressure not normal you need to chock the plane before you release'. Bluetooth headsets cut out and they did not hear the entire exchange. Airplane began to roll back with calls to 'set brakes set brakes set brakes'. Tow team was able to chock aircraft to stop movement with 5-6 feet. Aircraft stopped before we could activate yellow pump to return brake pressure. Return to the gate after brake pressure issue. Tug crew said to set parking brake. I sent parking brake and relayed to them that the parking brake was set and the pressure was not good. Evidently the Bluetooth headset cut out and he did not hear the last part. The aircraft rolled back approximately 6 feet. The chock was put in by maintenance to stop the aircraft. Brakes did not work. The chock stopped the aircraft before the FO or I could activate the yellow pump to get brake pressure back. No injuries and no damage to the aircraft or any facilities were noted. No contact with any other thing other than the chock.
ASRSN:2196284.s: During pushback, a brake pressure issue caused the aircraft to roll back six feet after the tug team failed to hear the crew's warning due to Bluetooth headset failure. Maintenance chocked the aircraft to stop movement before the crew could activate the yellow pump, resulting in no injuries or damage.

ASRSN:2196302.n: While level at 6000 we received a TCAS TA followed by an RA to 'monitor vertical speed'. Since we were level the guidance given by the FD (Flight Director) was to stay level. A small aircraft passed below us with an indicated 400 foot separation as shown on TCAS. The altimeters had been changing fairly quickly this day. We reported the RA to ATC and continued without incident.
ASRSN:2196302.s: The crew received a TCAS RA to monitor vertical speed while level at 6,000 feet, though the Flight Director indicated staying level. A small aircraft passed below with 400 feet of separation, attributed to rapidly changing altimeters, and the crew reported the event to ATC without incident.

ASRSN:2196303.n: Took off XXL in ZZZZ. After coming back to the cockpit after first break Captain notified me the aircraft taking off after us reported pieces of a tire on the runway. After several discussions with Dispatch and Maintenance there could be no confirmation that it was our aircraft was involved. As a precautionary measure crew decided to [request priority handling], request landing on XYR and have Crash Crew/Maintenance meet us after vacating the runway to do an inspection. We were told to proceed to the gate. After shutting down and completing the shutdown checklist we were notified that tires #7 was damaged. Normal predeparture from ZZZZ. On takeoff roll, unknown to us, #7 tire tread separated from tire. We had no indications of anything abnormal. Almost one hour after takeoff ZZZZ Control informed us that the subsequent departure had noticed tire debris on the runway. With no other indications and the distinct possibility that the debris was not from our aircraft, we continued the flight. We coordinated with Dispatch, maintenance, and chose to [request priority handling] on arrival with ZZZ Approach Control. Approach and landing were uneventful. After landing we stopped and had Fire/Rescue and Maintenance personnel inspect the landing gear. We then found out that our #7 tire had its tread missing (but was still inflated) and there was a dent in the flap panel above it. Taxied to gate and deplaned without issue.
ASRSN:2196303.s: The crew of an XXL departing ZZZZ continued flight after being informed of tire debris on the runway, as no in-flight indications existed. Post-landing inspection revealed the #7 tire tread had separated during takeoff, causing a dent in the flap panel, though the aircraft landed safely.

ASRSN:2196361.n: Employee on headset completed pushback and was awaiting command to disconnect the headset, when the aircraft unexpectedly released brakes and began to roll forward while employee still connected via headset to aircraft. Immediately contacted pilots who engaged the brakes. Shortly after, disconnect command was issued. Employee shaken but unharmed.
ASRSN:2196361.s: A ground employee on headset experienced an unexpected brake release and forward roll during pushback while still connected to the aircraft. The employee immediately contacted pilots who engaged the brakes; the employee was shaken but unharmed.

ASRSN:2196423.n: Taxing out for departure on ramp X in ZZZ, a baggage cart pulled out in front of us, After an abrupt stop fa's called to report injuries. After returning to the gate FA went to the hospital for a medical evaluation.Baggage cart pulled out in front of us. Upon taxi out from gate XX, northbound on Lane X, I observed a baggage cart tug crossing our path from left to right. In my assessment we were likely to impact the tug or come extremely uncomfortably close to it. I announced 'tug' to the CA and pointed in the direction of the tug. The CA was forced to brake hard to stop the aircraft. The tug continued and crossed our path with disregard. Moments later we were notified one of the flight attendants had been injured during the stop. I notified ramp control that we needed to return to the gate. I subsequently notified airport operations that emergency medical services were required. Someone get control of the overwhelming number of tug drivers that fly around the ramps with reckless abandon. All airports.
ASRSN:2196423.s: During taxi out from Gate XX, a baggage tug crossed the aircraft's path, forcing the captain to brake hard and causing a flight attendant injury. The crew returned to the gate for medical evaluation, attributing the incident to the tug driver's reckless disregard for safety.

ASRSN:2196451.n: During taxi out, Captain was taxing slower than normal due to taxiway conditions (1/4in wet snow 1/8 ice). Airplane handled appropriately. When cleared for take off XX aircraft was slowly taxied into position XX. When aircraft initially turned from heading Y towards heading X when the aircraft began to slide to the left of the runway. Captain tried to correct with nose steering and brakes. Neither were successful, the captain applied right thrust reverse to stop the unintentional slide to the left of the runway centerline. After the aircraft stopped the Captain the regained control through nose steering. Aircraft was positioned back to the centerline of XX and takeoff clearance was granted. Crew reported conditions to tower. Winter weather conditions made the approach end of XX less than reported values.
ASRSN:2196451.s: The Captain experienced an unintentional left slide during takeoff positioning on Runway XX due to wet snow and ice. Control was regained using right thrust reverse and nose steering, allowing the aircraft to return to the centerline for takeoff after reporting that actual conditions were worse than reported.

ASRSN:2196505.n: Climbing through approximately 25,000 ft., we received a HYD B LO LVL CAUTION, followed by HYD B LO PR just two minutes later. As we performed the appropriate ECAMs and checklists, ZZZ Center was trying to hand us off to ZZZ OCEANIC. At this point, we could see that we'd lost all hydraulic fluid from the BLUE system. In the interest of safety we decided not continue northbound into oceanic airspace. Instead, we decided to turn towards ZZZ. Once we were established southeast bound, we were able to report the problem to Dispatch via SATCOM, but the signal was weak and the call continually dropped. Also ACARS was inoperative due to the ATSU having been deferred.Once communication was reestablished with Dispatch and Maintenance Control, they recommended that we continue to ZZZ1 on the original flight plan. We felt that this was no longer an option as our Estimated Fuel On Board would've been 5,200 lbs at our ETA.While we were holding north of ZZZ we agreed with Dispatch to change our destination to ZZZ2 as the aircraft was then in a safe condition and the aircraft weight would be less than upon arrival in ZZZ2.We continued to ZZZ2, and the remainder of the flight was uneventful.
ASRSN:2196505.s: During climb through 25,000 ft., the crew lost all BLUE hydraulic fluid following HYD B caution lights. They diverted to ZZZ2 instead of continuing oceanic or landing at ZZZ1 due to low fuel estimates and communication issues caused by a deferred ATSU.

ASRSN:2196508.n: Due to winter ops, and per SOP the anti-ice switches were placed on during preflight. We then de-iced at ZZZ. Everything proceeded normally until shortly after takeoff when we received a master warning for the Left Wing A/Ice Fail. We completed the after takeoff checklist which includes turning the anti-ice switches back to auto. Once the wing anti-ice switch was turned to auto the master warning extinguished. We referenced the air synoptic page which showed the left wing anti-ice valve closed but amber. After a discussion, we elected to perform SOP wing anti-ice test above 10,000 feet hoping it would reset the valve. Placing the switch on again triggered the Left Wing A/Ice Fail EICAS and we completed the associated emergency checklist which has you turn the Wing Anti-Ice switch to off and exit/avoid icing conditions. We notified Dispatch through ACARS and began reviewing our options. The WSI (weather app) icing chart showed icing conditions at ZZZ1 and continuing well past our fuel reserves. We contacted dispatch via SATCOM and the decision was made to divert to ZZZ2 that was free of icing conditions. The flight continued uneventfully. A logbook entry was made upon arrival.
ASRSN:2196508.s: The flight crew experienced a Left Wing Anti-Ice Fail warning shortly after takeoff due to a closed valve. After a reset attempt failed, they diverted to ZZZ2 to avoid icing conditions and logged the fault upon arrival.

ASRSN:2196531.n: We were climbing from FL310 to FL350 for smoother ride. At about 34500 feet, we were hit by wake turbulence and at the same time TA alert went off. I pulled the speed brake out and put hands on throttle and yoke. I was ready to disconnect autothrottle and autoflight. Mach number increased from .78 to .82 for couple seconds. The wake passed, we leveled off at FL350 and told ATC about the wake. Landed in ZZZ, maintenance log filled, and had maintenance team checked out the jet. No damage was found. We flew the same jet later to ZZZ1. Our Purser called us during the encounter of the wake and stated his safety concerns for himself and passengers. Seatbelt sign was on when the event occurred. He told us passengers were at the aisle and he almost got hurt. We didn't know passengers were not complying with the seatbelt sign neither the cabin crew informed us before the event. Announcements were made whenever seatbelts sign turned on. We noticed the Purser was getting upset and emotional so my Captain asked the Purser to come to the cockpit so we can talk about the event but he refused. After we landed in ZZZ, Flight Attendant's Supervisor was involved and we had a conversation. We had no problem working together and continued the next flight to ZZZ1. CRM is one of the most important factors for flying safely. Stay calm and be professional are the foundation of a safe crew member. We descended to FL310 to avoid an area of reported turbulence in the ABQ sector. Once past the area we requested a climb back to FL330 initially as it was again reported smooth. During the climb ATC recommended and offered FL350 as it was also smooth and we accepted. At roughly 34300 feet we got a TCAS alert and that was immediately followed by a sudden jolt of turbulence and then an overspeed as we apparently went through the descending wake turbulence of an aircraft above. Flying pilot did a good job of immediately getting through speed brake out and I assisted by opening the speed window and lowering the set speed. At roughly Cost Index (CI) 40 - 50 we were initially climbing around Mach .78 and the aircraft accelerated to and slightly above the limit briefly. We got the aircraft back on path and made a report to ATC about the wake event. Made a maintenance entry. Inspection was completed in ZZZ and safe to continue next leg.During the wake event itself I got a chime from the flight attendants which I initially did not answer as we wanted the aircraft back on path and then got. 6 - 7 chimes rapidly as the event concluded. I informed the Flight Attendant (FA) I was dealing with an issue and would call right back. When I did the FA was irate, erratic, and using unprofessional language. My primary concern during this call was to determine if everyone was ok and that no one was hurt. I was assured that was the case. It was clear to me there was a breakdown in communication and general CRM and I requested that the Purser join us in the flight deck so we could have a face-to-face discussion in an attempt to repair. The Purser refused initially and said he needed some time. I said to just let me know when he was ready. We ended up debriefing with a FA Supervisor and the Purser before our next flight.
ASRSN:2196531.s: During a climb to FL350, the flight crew encountered wake turbulence and a TCAS alert, causing a brief overspeed to Mach .82. While no aircraft damage was found, the Purser reported passenger injuries and refused an immediate cockpit debrief due to unprofessional behavior, requiring later intervention by a supervisor.

ASRSN:2196557.n: On departure from ZZZ ceilings at 500 feet, assigned left turn to 050 while climbing to 2,000 feet. Engaged auto pilot at 700 feet AGL. Autopilot initiated the turn and continued the climb. Near 2,000 feet we observed the plane had banked past 30° and had continued turning past the assigned heading. There was a slight descent, and the lowest we observed was about 1,850 feet, and received a terrain alert. We took control of the aircraft, turned back to assigned heading and climbed back to 2,000 feet. We were then cleared to 3,000 and reengaged the auto pilot. It appeared that the auto pilot had disengaged without aural alert or visual red flashing 'AP' on the FMA (flight mode annunciator). Task saturation played a factor as we were climbing, turning, and receiving new frequencies while entering IMC through 500 feet.Suggestions: Continue procedure of Crew announcing FMA changes as they occur to enhance situational awareness. Continue to closely monitor desired versus actual flight path while using automation. Departed runway XX assigned a left turn heading 050. On departure engaged the autopilot at 700 feet AGL and initiated a left turn climbing to 2,000 feet. Shortly after was given a frequency change and told to contact departure. After checking in with departure noticed a slightly steeper than normal bank and a slow decent and saw the autopilot was no longer engaged. I immediately took control of the aircraft and leveled the wings and initiated a climb towards 2,000. At the same time we started climbing the terrain alert sounded, during the climb we went above 2,000 and were told to continue climbing to 3,000.Suggestions: In the future will be more vigilant on monitoring the FMA (flight mode annunciator) and not get distracted during times of higher workload so as to know without a doubt what the current condition of the aircraft and autopilot are.
ASRSN:2196557.s: Pilots reported that during departure in IMC, the autopilot disengaged without alert while turning to heading 050, causing an excessive bank and terrain alert near 1,850 feet. The crew manually recovered the aircraft, attributing the event to task saturation and a failure to monitor the flight mode annunciator.

ASRSN:2196574.n: Cleared for takeoff, I was PF. At 80 knots, the FO called out '80' to which I replied 'checked.' At 100 knots, the FO said what I thought was 'I got no airspeed.' I replied 'what?' He said 'my airspeed is dead, abort.' At this point we were approaching v1, and I decided to abort the takeoff rather than try and asses further and risk hitting v1 (and thus requiring a takeoff and potential in flight emergency of unreliable airspeed). Upon clearing the runway, the flight attendants had already walked through the cabin and verified everyone was okay. We returned to the gate without further incidentCause: Possible de ice fluid in pitot tubes.
ASRSN:2196574.s: The Pilot Flying aborted the takeoff at 100 knots after the First Officer reported dead airspeed, fearing unreliable airspeed near V1. The crew returned to the gate safely, attributing the failure to possible de-ice fluid in the pitot tubes.

ASRSN:2196583.n: Visual approach to runway XX. ATIS reported Rwy XX PAPI low intensity out of service". There was no PAPI visible. Captain was hand flying. Around 400 feet I noted that we were well below glideslope to the Captain. More than 1 dot low. He said "visual, continue". We continued the approach, landed, exited the runway at Y taxiway, and proceeded to the gate.PAPI out of service.Stay on the electronic glideslope rather than flying visually."
ASRSN:2196583.s: During a visual approach to runway XX with the PAPI out of service, the First Officer noted the aircraft was more than one dot below the glideslope at 400 feet while the Captain was hand-flying. The Captain elected to continue visually, resulting in a landing and the reporter's recommendation to stay on the electronic glideslope instead.

ASRSN:2196584.n: On final approach to ZZZ at 170 KTS, cleared the visual approach for XX at 4000 feet. The aircraft captured the Localizer and then captured Glide Slope approaching the ZZZZZ Fix. Suddenly the Auto Pilot pitched up the aircraft 7-8 degrees. Once the it was obvious it was not an oscillation, the FO disconnected the autopilot and leveled the plane at 4,350. Informed approach of potential interference with the glide slope and hand flew the approach and landing. Captain wrote up the autopilot with details of the incident.An aircraft taxied into position and took off while on approach, possibly causing glide slope interference. While not an unusual situation on visual approach, this particular aircraft did have a more severe reaction than most.Attempt to react faster to aggressive autopilot excursions to minimize deviations. On final approach to ZZZ at 170 KTS, the aircraft Auto Pilot captured the Localizer and then captured the Glide Slope approaching the ZZZZZ Fix at 4,000' MSL as Normal. At approximately 1-2 miles from ZZZZZ, the Auto Pilot pitched up the aircraft 7-8 degrees above the normal configured pitch of 3-5 degrees with small buffeting beginning. The FO disconnected the AP and leveled the plane at 4,350' MSL and then hand flew an uneventful approach and landing.We queried the tower if there were any reports of Glide Slope oscillations on the approach to XX and they replied Negative. They then queried other aircraft following us.There was one large aircraft that that rolled onto the runway and took off prior to our final approach portion of our flight.The Autopilot Caused the excessive Nose Up Pitch, with contributing factors of some type of malfunction in the Autopilot System and potentially Glide Slope Signal interference from the ground.Landing on Runway XX at ZZZ with traffic crossing the runway, taking off, and landing prior to our aircraft causes wavering in the ILS signals and resulting wavering in the Autopilot on approach.The aircraft was Written Up for a discrepancy with Autopilot to ensure it is fully functional and hopefully the other aircraft that followed us reported any discrepancy with ILS Signals.
ASRSN:2196584.s: During a visual approach to ZZZ, the autopilot pitched the aircraft up 7-8 degrees near the ZZZZZ fix, likely due to glide slope interference from a departing aircraft or an autopilot malfunction. The First Officer disconnected the autopilot, leveled the plane at 4,350 feet, and hand-flew a safe landing while the aircraft was written up for the discrepancy.

ASRSN:2196601.n: Approaching PGD VMC conditions at night after Tower closure from the north along the LUBBR arrival, I was assigned direct to CISTS to setup for the visual for rwy 04. I had the airport in sight and PM advised Approach around 10-8 NM from PGD and we were cleared for the visual. Initially I began to widen out to more of a downwind and attempt to turn a perpendicular base to CISTS and continued a descent to 1,600 ft. I believe my error at this point was that I was equating similar night experience at PIE airport with this shorter approach and I became too disoriented trying to keep the airport in sight over my shoulder along with navigating to an unfamiliar approach fix. I asked PM to re-enter direct CISTS to join the approach and my initial thought was that we would be too high at 1,600 feet. I continued a descent first selecting 1,000 and open descent as we began to turn onto the final approach path.PM appropriately spoke up being more familiar with the area saying he felt too low. My initial attempt to level off I believe I tried to scroll in the next 100 ft altitude and pull but I don't know the actual altitude that I entered. We then received a low energy 'speed speed' caution. I decided to transition fully to visual and disconnected autopilot and requested FD off and bird on. Once we were leveled with Autothrust on speed we were at 1,000 ft and below GS with an aural glide slope caution until re intercepting an on glide path condition. From there I continued to a normal landing. I believe given this was my second approach to PGD at night in the last year, a more complete straight in approach would have been better in assisting me to gain familiarity. Operating at an uncontrolled field and wanting to make a visual approach despite my lack of recent experience contributed to this undesired aircraft state. Lastly I feel some fatigue was at play as well.
ASRSN:2196601.s: The pilot and PM experienced a low energy state and glide slope deviation while conducting a night visual approach to PGD. The pilot attributed the incident to disorientation, lack of recent experience, fatigue, and an inappropriate attempt to widen the approach path.

ASRSN:2196748.n: We were performing a test which requires engine high power runup on taxiway 1. Escorted by airport ops. After completing engine run up we gave follow me truck signal by blinking taxi lights that we are ready to go 'no direct communication' so the follow me truck immediately made 180 degree turn from the same exact taxiway. We tried to make 180 degree turn without hitting taxiway edge light 'edge lights were inop' after excessive turn steering inop and the steering stopped responding. we immediately put throttle to idle and applied brakes . No direct communication between us and escort truck . Less visibility and snowing two way communication have been maintained.
ASRSN:2196748.s: During a high-power engine runup on Taxiway 1 in snow, the crew signaled a follow-me truck to turn 180 degrees without direct communication. While attempting the turn, the aircraft's steering failed, forcing an immediate stop with brakes and idle thrust to avoid inoperative edge lights.

ASRSN:2196785.n: Twice in the last week AGS has had to go ATC Limited or ATC Zero due to lines being cut and stolen for copper. When the lines are cut AGS loses primary radar, multiple frequencies, and shout lines. When ATC limited and VFR Tower only we have to work off a PET 2000 (Portable Emergency Transceiver) for LC (Local Control). Additionally, one of the PETs had poor range and would cut out mid transmission. Then led to unsafe handling of A/C when we had 4 HELOs and an air carrier on frequency and we could not give traffic due to transmissions not going out. Recommendations - the telecommunication lines need to be buried and protected, and or move the Tower to the other side of the field with the lines buried and protected.
ASRSN:2196785.s: AGS controllers faced ATC Limited or Zero status twice due to stolen copper lines cutting primary radar and communications. A faulty PET 2000 caused transmission failures during mixed helicopter and air carrier traffic, preventing traffic advisories and creating unsafe handling conditions.

ASRSN:2196804.n: Currently there are 2 published approaches to Runway 31 in LGA with the same designation. Park Visual 31 approach plate indicates that it is selectable as RNVX 31, and RNAV (GPS) X 31-INDUSTRY is also selectable as RNVX 31. When selecting RNVX 31 approach, the database loads up the RNAV (GPS) X 31-INDUSTRY approach. There is not any way to load the Park Visual approach. Both approaches are overlays. However, they use different fixes and different missed approach procedures. This discrepancy can lead to confusion on the flight deck, especially when planning such an unusual approach.
ASRSN:2196804.s: A pilot reported that at LGA, two distinct Runway 31 approaches share the RNVX 31 designation, causing the FMS to load the RNAV (GPS) X 31-INDUSTRY instead of the Park Visual approach. This database discrepancy prevents loading the Park Visual procedure and creates flight deck confusion due to differing fixes and missed approach paths.

ASRSN:2196837.n: After landing in CMH, we were holding short of Gate XXX on the E apron inner loop taxiway. A [An air carrier aircraft] landed behind us and was going to Gate XXY. As we were holding short of the Gate the [other aircraft] asked Ground if they could taxi to the right of us and proceed to Gate XXY. Ground said the ramp was an uncontrolled area and the [other aircraft] continued to taxi to Gate XXY passing on our right (west side) cutting through parking spot XXX, coming very close to our wing with no wing walkers and what I felt was a very unsafe speed.
ASRSN:2196837.s: After landing at CMH, our aircraft held short of Gate XXX while another carrier aircraft requested and received permission to taxi right of us through an uncontrolled ramp area. The other aircraft passed close to our wing at an unsafe speed without wing walkers, cutting through parking spot XXX to reach Gate XXY.

ASRSN:2196847.n: We were flying north from ZZZ just south of ZZZ1. The number 2 engine filter bypass light illuminated. The First Officer was the PF, so I referenced and actioned the QRH. The filter bypass light checklist is very short, and as we would be reducing thrust in an engine and possibly shutting down, I immediately requested a descent to FL310. After retarding the thrust, the bypass light became intermittent at varying amounts of thrust. I then notified Dispatch and coordinated with my Dispatcher and Maintenance. Maintenance advised me to follow the QRH, but with an intermittent light gave me oil pressure and temperature parameters to monitor. After descending to FL 270 and being cleared to descend via the ZZZZZ the bypass light became steady and I noted an increase in oil temperature we elected to [request priority handling] and shut down the engine per the QRH Engine Shutdown checklist. The checklist calls for landing at the nearest suitable airport. As we were already cleared to descend and had briefed the arrival into ZZZ3 we decided that ZZZ3 would be the best option for landing and would prevent the introduction of new threats inherent in a diversion. I briefed the flight attendants with no special instructions and no further issues expected after landing. We descended via the ZZZZZ arrival, I took over the flying duties and landed uneventfully on Runway XXR in ZZZ3. We taxied to Gate and deplaned normally. Maintenance write up was completed and Chief Pilot called for debrief.
ASRSN:2196847.s: The Captain and First Officer experienced a steady number 2 engine filter bypass light and rising oil temperature while descending to FL270. They shut down the engine per the QRH and landed uneventfully at ZZZ3, avoiding a diversion.

ASRSN:2196854.n: While conducting pre-flight duties in ZZZ, a planned Dangerous Goods (DG) summary printed. The planned DG called for 0 lb. of dry ice in the OFF" position. 10 minutes prior to departure, the ground crew communicated they were ready for brake release and pushback. I asked the ground crew to send the final DG summary, but they stated no DG was loaded. I contacted the Dispatcher and stated that we had received a planned DG summary, but no final DG summary. The Dispatcher contacted Load Planning, and informed me that no DG had been loaded and that we were good to go. After departing ZZZ, I sent Load Planning an ACARS message asking why a final DG summary had not been sent. The Load Planner stated "DG was not loaded, it was held off by Cargo, that's why you did not get a DG summary. I sent you a copy of it showing held off." Following that message, a final DG summary printed showing no DG was loaded."
ASRSN:2196854.s: The flight crew at ZZZ received a planned Dangerous Goods summary indicating dry ice, but ground and dispatch confirmed no cargo was loaded. A final summary printed after departure clarified the item was held off by Cargo, resolving the discrepancy.

ASRSN:2197036.n: We had an emergency landing on our flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 and had to divert to ZZZ. During landing after preparing cabin for arrival and both FAs (Flight Attendants) sitting in our jump seats, the CA called us to inform he and the FO heard strange clicking noises from the nose gear when the landing gear was activated. To be on the safe side he told us we would go around and try again and see if they continued to hear those sounds. If the sounds were heard again we would divert to ZZZ and need to prepare the cabin for an emergency landing. Shortly after we went around to try again he called us on the call and told us the sounds continued so we were diverting and would have to prepare for an emergency landing. He asked if 10 minutes would be enough to prepare for the planned emergency landing and we said it was enough time.After receiving the call for an emergency landing we both quickly retrieved our emergency landing checklist from underneath our jump seats and met in the fwd galley. We turned all the lights to bright and followed the checklist. The Purser did demos in the aisle while I did the announcement. After the announcements we went through the proper procedures including making sure everyone knew their brace position and brace command, where the nearest exits were, and when and how to evacuate if it came down to that. ABPs (Able-bodied Passengers) were also briefed on doors in case of an evacuation. We remained calm and collective while still keeping a sense of urgency. We made sure questions and concerns were addressed and reassured the pax that were scared.After preparing the cabin and completing our checklist I returned to my jumpseat and called the Purser to notify her that I was secure. We waited for the Captain to give the brace command and when he did we began giving our brace commands loud and clear. We safely landed and the captain made an announcement that everything was safe and that we would be taxing to the gate to deplane. I checked for any fire, debris, or smoke outside of the windows just in case. We arrived at the gate and safely got all of the pax off. We collected our things and got off as well as maintenance came on to check plane.
ASRSN:2197036.s: Flight attendants prepared the cabin for an emergency landing after the Captain and First Officer heard clicking noises from the nose gear during two landing attempts. The aircraft diverted and landed safely, with maintenance inspecting the plane after all passengers deplaned.

ASRSN:2197047.n: Near Mid Air Collision 5 nm SW of the SAX VOR. Within Mode C veil did not see traffic on ADS-B or visually until close, took necessary action to avoid.
ASRSN:2197047.s: A pilot reported a near mid-air collision 5 nm SW of the SAX VOR within the Mode C veil. Traffic was not seen on ADS-B or visually until close, requiring the pilot to take avoidance action.

ASRSN:2197055.n: Approach runway XX LOC at minimum runway was not in sight. At missed approach point pilot not flying (GO missed ), (pilot flying) advised ATC going missed and ATC replied missed as published except 15,000 ft pilot flying confirmed. Pilot flying did not execute the missed approach on point and did not turn as published and climb rate was lower than supposed which lead to getting closer to the mountain. And ATC advised to turn left to rejoin the missed heading of 300 because terrain on the right side is more than 14,000 ft and airplane altitude is 12,000 ft. After pilot turned left TCAS alert traffic which it was another airplane going missed behind us, so ATC advised to climb 16,000 ft to avoid it, then diverted to ZZZ and landed safely.
ASRSN:2197055.s: During a missed approach, the pilot flying failed to execute the published procedure, resulting in low altitude near terrain and a TCAS alert from a trailing aircraft. ATC issued vectoring and climb instructions to avoid terrain and traffic, leading to a safe diversion and landing.

ASRSN:2197059.n: During night visual approach 28L SFO. At night so hard to say exact distance, but I feel we got too close to a C-17 cargo jet. Felt some of his wake turbulence. The autopilot overshot intercepting the localizer and FO had to intervene a bit to turn harder to intercept to avoid the C-17 on a parallel visual to 28R.I should have intervened sooner to avoid getting so close to the C-17.
ASRSN:2197059.s: During a night visual approach to SFO 28L, the crew encountered wake turbulence from a nearby C-17 on a parallel visual to 28R after the autopilot overshot the localizer intercept. The First Officer intervened to turn harder to avoid the C-17, though the pilot felt they should have acted sooner to prevent the close proximity.

ASRSN:2197064.n: My client, the pilot flying, and I, the flight instructor, were practicing the VOR-B approach into ZZZ. The conditions were VMC and we began the approach at the ZZZ IAF at 3,000 MSL and were cleared for the approach at some point on the initial approach segment. My client began a descent down to 2,300, the minimum altitude on that segment of the procedure, and ZZZ [Approach] gave us permission to switch over to the common traffic advisory frequency somewhere outside of ZZZZZ, the intermediate fix. Upon crossing ZZZZZ, my client began a descent to MDA. Neither of us realized at first that we had begun a descent prior to the FAF, thinking that ZZZZZ was instead the final approach fix. As I preceded to make a radio call to local traffic I noticed the distance change on the GPS and realized that we had actually just crossed the final approach fix several hundred feet below the minimum altitude. The weather conditions were VMC and we could see that there were no obstacles so we levelled off and then executed the missed approach procedure. Upon contacting ATC on the missed approach, the controller advised us that he had gotten an altitude alert and that we had to maintain 2,300 MSL until crossing the FAF. We agreed and acknowledged that we were aware and would not let that happen again. At first I was not exactly sure how either of us had missed the mistake. I've been flying professionally for many years and had flown for the airline as a First Officer and Captain for most of those years. I put strong emphasis on a sterile cockpit and there we no unusual circumstances or distractions during the event. In the debriefing we discussed the possibilities as to what had caused the error and it may have been an instance of confirmation bias. Prior to the flight we had briefed performing the procedure turn at ZZZZZ, which also served as an IAF, and I noted that ATC rarely assigned ZZZ as the IAF as I had done the approach many times before.
